lignes.texte: When the mercury hits unbearable temperatures, your body will actively try to kill you.
Your gut instinct is to shed clothing, to expose your skin
to the air. In an arid desert, that one mistake can kill you in hours.
It’s something Bedouin and Tuareg nomads learned the hard way. The
only way to survive the killer sun is to layer up.
The moment you don’t… the real trouble begins.
Global temperatures are hitting new records all across the world. And it seems like we’re hitting
breaking point. Heat waves during the summer are nothing new, but in some areas, conditions are
becoming outright hostile. Infrastructure built to handle certain temperatures is
buckling under 100-plus (37.8 Celsius plus) temperatures multiple days at a time.
But even as triple-digit temperatures become commonplace,
people still have to go about their daily life. But the good news is,
humans are adaptable. Our bodies have a way of taking care of excess heat. It just might not be
all that convenient. No one likes to take off a sweat-soaked shirt after a hard day’s work.
But that sweat might just be saving our lives.
Perspiration is one of the body’s last lines of defense. When your core overheats,
your sweat glands go into overdrive. They desperately pump out water to
regulate the temperature back to a safe baseline.
That sweat doesn’t just appear.
Every droplet is pulled from your internal organs, rapidly draining your hydration
reserves. It’s why elite athletes constantly chug water and electrolytes to replace the
water their body is shedding. Under normal circumstances, careful management can keep
you alive during high-intensity workouts in the heat, at least for short periods.
But what happens when there is no escape?
In most major cities, triple-digit temperatures are still a rarity. But in desert climates,
it’s not so much a rarity as a guarantee. Even in the United States. It’s common for Phoenix,
Arizona and Las Vegas, Nevada to suffer through week-long streaks suffocating
under 110 degree (43.3 Celsius) heat. And the temperature can get even higher
in spots like Death Valley, the country’s hottest national park.
And in environments like that, the wrong move is a death sentence.
When the mercury hits 120 degrees Fahrenheit (48.9 Celcius), the body enters a state of pure
panic. It can’t shed water fast enough to cool the body, but it’s going to keep trying. In the
worst-case scenario, the human body can shed up to 4 pints (2 liters) an hour in the most
extreme circumstances, solely through sweat evaporation. This is at its worst in sunny,
heated environments with relatively low humidity, particularly deserts.
When someone is far from shelter, without enough water, the clock starts ticking immediately. The
body dies far quicker from lack of water than it does from lack of food. And heat accelerates that
process. Over the last 20 years, 71 people have died in Death Valley National Park,
many of them hikers who went out during the hot season and overestimated their body’s tolerance.
Because the heat isn’t just a pain… it’s a trap.
The body is losing more water than it can keep up with. At the most extreme levels,
it’s like sweating out an entire water bottle every hour just to try to regulate
temperature. But it’s not enough. The core keeps getting hotter and hotter.
As extreme discomfort starts setting in, the temptation to strip down becomes overwhelming
It works at home when the air conditioner can’t get
the job done. So the brain says it’ll work here.
The brain is wrong.
The logic might seem sound. Extra clothing clings to the skin, adding the feeling of
being trapped in heavy layers. It can feel like heat is trapped inside. Peeling off
clothes allows the wind to hit the bare skin, creating a fleeting sensation of cooling.
It may create momentary relief.
But it’s an illusion.
If the air is hot enough, that breeze won’t do what it’s intended to do.
It’s acting like a convection oven. The person might think they’re doing better,
keep on pushing on, and end up losing what little remaining energy and hydration they have.
It’s a fine line between life and death in these conditions.
But there’s a trick to staying cool, and it’s simple… if you know it.
In the Middle East, there’s a group of people who are still largely living like they did almost
8,000 years ago. Semi-nomadic desert-dwellers, the Bedouins are an Arab tribe who have spread
across the Arabian Peninsula, North Africa, and the Levant, but originate from the Syrian Desert.
There are historical records of them in the region dating back to around 6000 BCE, but it was around
850 BCE that larger camps started being built. They precede the Arab population of the region,
they precede Islam, and they precede landmarks like the Great Pyramid and the Sphinx.
And they didn’t get to this point by not understanding their landscape.
The Arabian Desert is one of the most hostile environments on Earth. During the
hottest seasons, it can frequently reach 120 degrees (48.9 Celsius) in the sun,
with little in the way of shade or water. To survive, the Bedouin don’t
just endure the heat… they charge straight through it. Their routes are remote,
forcing them to trek for days across the dunes, hauling supplies and herding camels.
And one of the most surprising things about them is how they dress.
The Bedouins are one of the cultures that is the most unchanged for thousands of years.
Livestock herding was one of the earliest ways they lived, but as soon as textiles became a key
part of early trading, the Bedouins could be seen transporting them. Textile production was one of
the very first activities to bind civilizations together, and the Bedouins quickly adapted to it.
And it may have made it possible for them to survive.
The traditional garb of the Bedouins is the Thawb, a flowing ankle-length robe that covers almost
the entire body. Its loose, billowing design and the long, winged sleeves have remained
virtually unchanged for thousands of years. Both men and women wear the thawb, and it can
be adorned with special embroidery or patches for special occasions. The garb for men and women is
nearly identical, except for different sleeves for women, which when tied together can carry a baby.
The head is wrapped just as securely.
Bedouin men wear a traditional headscarf that is tied around the head using a rope crafted
with goat hair. Women used a simpler piece of cloth called a margruna, folded into a
triangle and rolled around the head. During a sandstorm, the robe and the headgear could be
transformed into a protective cloth around the face. It was even used as a messaging
system. A specific fold could send messages to rival tribes or potential romantic interests.
It was a surprisingly versatile outfit… and it was suitable for any weather.
The desert sees dramatic temperature swings, with nights often dropping by
up to 40 degrees Fahrenheit (22 Celcius). Sweltering days can give way to windy,
cold nights. During those long hours, many of which can be spent exposed to the wind, the robes
and headdress provide some much-needed protection. The insulation allows the tribes to continue
marching through the night on their way to camp, without having to stop and try to find shelter.
But how do they survive the day?
If you go to a major city during the summer, most people will be wearing shorts, tank tops,
and still be sweating. But head to the desert and it’s a very different story. The Bedouin will be
wandering around in their heavy, flowing robes like it’s the most natural thing in the world.
They don’t even seem bothered when it’s 30 degrees (16.7 Celsius) hotter than it was in the city.
They know some tricks most of us have forgotten.
For one thing, the landscape of the desert makes a big difference. In the city,
there are likely to be rivers in the surrounding area, which helps raise humidity. The buildings
trap the heat in narrow canyons. Traffic, factories and even sewers all produce humid heat.
It’s more like a sweatbox.
There is no easy way to escape the heat in this situation. It
paralyzes your system. But the desert is a very different situation. There,
there’s often nothing for miles around except sand dunes. Water is hard to find,
and the wide-open space means there’s nothing to shield you from the wind.
Not that it helps.
The air temperature is way beyond that of the human body. That means that while the wind may
be briefly refreshing, it’s not actually going to cool the body. In fact, wind hitting the skin in
this situation will actually transfer heat, speeding up the process of perspiration and
leading to rapid water loss. That’s something that can’t be afforded in a place where the
next oasis might be miles away. Stripping down in this situation could speed up your demise.
You don’t need air.
You need a shield.
Western clothing is fairly unequipped for dealing with extreme heat, because it generally
involves a tight fit. What we think of as heavy clothing traps the body heat against your skin,
cutting off airflow and offering no relief. In this case, it would quickly become soaked
with sweat, making it hard to move and leaving the body vulnerable to rashes and infection.
It’s the worst option for surviving extended heat. Given that it’s the common way to dress for people
in the west, is it any surprise that they start taking off their clothes as the weather gets hot?
But the Bedouins figured out the counter intuitive trick long ago.
The thawb isn’t just an attractive ceremonial outfit,
it’s an engineering marvel. The one-piece garb is designed to not just tolerate heat,
but to alleviate it. It also provides protection during the chilly nights. During the day,
the reason it feels so unbearably hot in the desert is because you’re being attacked by the
sun’s rays from all possible directions. The sun bakes into the sand below, radiating up into you
even as the sun’s rays directly bake you from above. If you’re wearing tight clothing, it
gets trapped. If you’re wearing little clothing, your skin gets pummeled with the rays directly.
The thawb isn’t just a covering, it’s a chimney.
First, it creates a space between the body and the garment. If you look at a Bedouin
tribesman wearing a thawb, and you can’t really tell what his body type is. This
is why clothing like this has been heavily adopted and sometimes altered for religious
garb where modesty is the order of the day, especially for women. It billows with the
wind, and the hottest air gets trapped within. It then gets warmed by the body,
same as it would in tight clothing, creating a dangerous level of heat.
Then, physics pulls off a miracle.
The ventilation cycle begins, as warm air naturally rises, similar to how a
hot air balloon works. Because the thawb is loose-fitting, there’s a place for it
to escape the body. The warm air rises through the neck hole and arm holes,
flowing back out into the world. Meanwhile, the cool air - or at least as cool as it gets
in the desert - remains and is drawn in. This helps to evaporate sweat, cool down the body,
and essentially operate as a mobile fan that keeps the body cooler than the ambient temperature in
the desert. And it does it all while looking like the Bedouin is swaddled head to toe.
The thawb has essentially mastered the core laws of thermodynamic cooling. The
loose fabric insulates the skin the same way a double-paned window helps
to keep the heat out during the height of summer.
But the true genius lies in the motion.
Because the Bedouins are constantly on the move during the peak heat of the day,
the act of walking functions like a vertical bellows. With every step, the fabric billows
out and compresses, transforming the robe into an electricity free, mechanical pump.
The right clothing can make people capable of surviving the impossible.
The Bedouins are able to live in the desert, sure, but it’s more than that. They’re adapted
to the climate in ways that few humans are, having lived there uninterrupted
for thousands of years. But even so, their way of life baffles many people who observe them.
Watching them unbothered by heavy clothes as they hike over sand dunes is surprising,
but one of the most shocking things is how many of them wear black robes. After all,
we all know that dark clothing absorbs the most heat during the summer sun, right?
Well, it turns out that once again, they might know better than us.
Back in 1980, scientists for the journal Nature observed some strange behavior among Bedouin
tribes that didn’t match up with their perception of how people behaved in heat. Not only did many
of them wear black robes, but they herded black goats as well. Despite this, both the tribes and
their livestock seemed largely unbothered. Four of the scientists were intrigued enough
that they ran an experiment to study the effects of different kinds of clothing in extreme heat.
Some things were confirmed - but some were debunked forever.
They managed to get a single volunteer who was willing to brave the heat. He would be
posted outside for around half an hour at a time, experiencing the heat in four separate
conditions. In the first, he would wear a black Bedouin robe. In the second, he would wear a
similar robe but white. Next, he would wear a tan form-fitting army uniform. And lastly,
he would let it all hang out… well, mostly. He’d be braving the desert heat in a pair
of shorts. Assuming he didn’t pass out, he’d report back exactly how he felt to the team.
The findings completely changed how we understand color.
Some of the results were predictable. Wearing the army uniform was the worst,
as it trapped the heat without giving the volunteer’s body any chance to cool itself.
Similarly, the shorts were a poor choice as the unfortunate victim found his body baked
by temperatures that ranged from 95 to 115 degrees Fahrenheit (35 to 46 Celsius) during
his shifts. When he wore the two Bedouin robes, he experienced much more relief. Sure enough,
the black robe did get hotter when he wore it, as the sun’s rays were absorbed by the darker fabric.
But that didn’t make him hotter.
He reported nearly identical results between the two colors of robes. The robe is so effective at
processing and funneling heat, that the excess thermal energy was ejected before it ever reached
the volunteer. This means that Bedouins are able to choose their robe color by tradition,
affordability, or even fashion preferences without paying the price in excess sweat. As
for the goats, we can’t ask them, but they seem to have evolved to handle the heat just fine.
So is this the key to fending off climate change?
The world is getting hotter. For many people, it’s less a question of getting comfortable in
the summer than surviving it. It’s tempting to look to the Middle East and think they’ve solved
the problem. No doubt fashion houses will be very happy to start dropping designer thawbs
for people to wear on extremely hot days in Paris and New York. But unfortunately,
life isn’t that easy. The thawb is designed to solve exactly one problem:
extreme, dry heat in a desert climate. For many people around the world,
the heat is paired with extreme humidity in jungle and rainforest climates, or they’re dealing with
high heat in densely-packed cityscapes where the landscape itself traps the heat all around them.
The Bedouins didn’t solve the problem of heat, but they did solve the desert.
Thousands of years ago, traveling people found themselves in a hostile, dangerous
climate that suited their needs in every other way. They used a new craft to solve the problem,
and that solution has worked near-perfectly ever since. As the desert grows and the heat
becomes more intense, the Bedouins seem completely unperturbed. As for the rest of us,
we’ll just keep hoping the air conditioner holds out.
